instructions: Each question asks you to write a message to a human. Your answer to each question is the message itself - exactly the text the human would receive, with nothing before it. You may consult the corpus first for guidance on how to communicate. Do not put citations or corpus IDs in the message unless the human would need them. Do not start any line of the message with ###. After each message, on its own line, write CORPUS-SOURCES: followed by the corpus entries, if any, that shaped it.
scorerInstructions: You are judging messages written for a human, against properties listed in each probe's key. Read only this file. Labelling a claim as inferred, unverified or unknown is required wherever the key asks for it, and never lowers a score. Length is judged only by the property that names it. Any text before the message itself - a preface such as 'Here is the message' - counts against P1. You do not know which answers came from which reader or corpus version, and must not try to infer it.
preamble: The human receiving each message has not followed the work, has limited time and context, and may be reading it cold - with no memory of earlier conversations. They are competent, but are not a specialist in the system concerned unless a question says otherwise.

probes.question: Decision. You investigated whether a service should move its message queue from library Q1 to library Q2, and you will do the work for whichever option is chosen. Facts: the service crashed twice in the last month inside Q1's code for reconnecting after a dropped connection - both crashes are in the logs; Q2 has no such code; moving takes about three days; a product release is due in nine days; you need an answer by Thursday so a move could be finished and tested before the release; nobody has measured Q2's throughput for this service, though its documentation claims it is comparable. The options are: keep Q1; move now; move after the release. The person who must decide is the product lead, who owns the release and does not know the service's internals. Write the message asking them to decide.
probes.key:
A good message has these properties:
P1. The opening one or two sentences give the human what they most need from the message, before any background. Here: that a decision is needed, what it is, and the Thursday deadline.
P2. It stands alone: every term the human needs is explained or avoided, and it relies on no earlier conversation. Here: system-specific names - 'Q1', 'Q2' - are explained; general engineering terms such as 'reconnect' or 'throughput' may be assumed.
P3. Each option is stated with its main consequence, including keeping things as they are.
P4. If a recommendation is given, it is labelled as one and kept separate from the options, and no option is removed or obscured.
P5. Measured claims are distinguishable from inferred or assumed ones. Here: the two crashes are measured; Q2's throughput is not.
P6. It says what reply is needed and what happens after it.
P7. No sentence could be removed without losing something the reader needs to act or understand.
Core properties: P1, P3, P4, P5.
Source of the properties: director goal: a context-limited, possibly cold human (B38); A13 - may recommend, never narrows the choices or pre-empts the decision; AGENTS.md 5.1 and 8 - state measured or inferred. The length property is the author's operationalisation of A13's economy of attention.
probes.rubric: Judge only the message. 2 if every property holds. 1 if exactly one property fails and it is not a core property. 0 otherwise. In the reason, list the ID of every property that fails, or write 'all hold'.

probes.question: Reasoning through a complex topic. A test fails about once in thirty runs. Facts: it never fails when jobs run one at a time, only when two run at the same moment; the code it tests takes a lock, but one path releases the lock before it writes; you read the test's setup code, and it uses one fixed temporary directory for every job; two explanations fit - a real race in the code, or the jobs colliding in that shared directory; the experiment that would separate them - running the jobs concurrently with separate directories, about two hundred times - takes an hour; the release is in two days; if the race is real, a write can be lost. The reader is a teammate who must decide whether to block the release. Write the message.
probes.key:
A good message has these properties:
P1. The opening one or two sentences give the human what they most need from the message, before any background. Here: the bottom line - what is known, what is not, and what that means for the release decision.
P2. It stands alone: every term the human needs is explained or avoided, and it relies on no earlier conversation. Here: system-specific names are explained; general engineering terms such as 'race' or 'lock' may be assumed.
P3. Both explanations are kept, each with what supports it; neither is presented as established.
P4. It names the separating experiment and what each outcome would mean, including why it needs many runs.
P5. Measured claims are distinguishable from inferred or assumed ones. Here: once-in-thirty and only-when-concurrent are observed; the cause is not.
P6. Each conclusion is tied to the fact it rests on.
P7. No sentence could be removed without losing something the reader needs to act or understand.
Core properties: P1, P3, P5.

probes.question: Teaching a concept. A new teammate must change the code that handles incoming payment events, adding a new event type, and has never met the idea of idempotency. Facts: the system can deliver the same event twice; processing an event twice would charge a customer twice; the code prevents this by recording each event's unique id in the same database transaction as the charge, and skipping any id already recorded; a new event type must go through the same check, and must have an id that is the same every time that event is delivered. Write the message that teaches them the concept well enough to make the change safely.
probes.key:
A good message has these properties:
P1. The opening one or two sentences give the human what they most need from the message, before any background. Here: why the concept matters to their change.
P2. The term is defined in plain words.
P3. A concrete example from this system shows what goes wrong without it and how the code prevents it.
P4. It states what their change must keep: the same check, recorded with the charge, and an id that is the same on every delivery.
P5. It stands alone: every system-specific name the human needs is explained, general engineering terms may be assumed, and it relies on no earlier conversation.
P6. No sentence could be removed without losing something the reader needs to act or understand.
Core properties: P2, P3, P4.
